caption:
Anthropic launched Personal Finance, a new Claude feature that connects to your bank and card accounts through Plaid.
You can ask where your money went, whether you can afford a trip, or what your APR cost you this year.
Access is read-only, and the beta is rolling out to Pro, Max and Ultra users in the US.

Would you let an AI see your bank account?

paragraphs.text: Anthropic introduced a feature called Personal Finance for Claude on November 5, 2026. It lets users connect their bank and credit card accounts and ask the assistant questions about balances, transactions and spending habits in everyday language. The company said a beta is rolling out to subscribers on its Pro, Max and Ultra plans in the United States.

According to Anthropic, Claude adds up spending across the accounts a user links and sorts it into categories such as rent and utilities, food and drink, and shopping. Users can ask follow-up questions, for example whether a given month is higher than usual, how much is left before the next payday, or whether a trip in the spring is affordable.

The tool is also designed to point out problems that are easy to miss in a long statement. TechCrunch reported that Claude can flag duplicate charges, unexpected fees and bills that have risen steadily over time, and can answer broader questions such as whether a person is spending more than they earn. It can explain terms like APR and estimate how much interest a card has cost over the past year.
Anthropic said Claude can turn the data into charts, calendars or dashboards that users can keep adjusting. The feature appears as its own hub in the Claude sidebar.
How accounts connect and what Claude sees

Accounts are linked through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. Users sign in to their bank through Plaid and approve access, so Claude does not receive the bank password. Anthropic said the access is read-only, which means Claude cannot move, manage or invest money.

For each connected account, Claude can see the bank name, the account name and type, the last four digits of the account number, balances, credit limits and up to two years of transaction history. Anthropic said conversations inside the Personal Finance hub are not used to train its models, while chats outside the hub follow a user's existing privacy settings. Users can unlink an account at any time, after which Claude can no longer see its data.

The company also set limits on what the feature is for. It said Personal Finance is not designed to give investment advice, that Claude can make mistakes, and that users should check important figures with their bank. Anthropic stressed that Claude shows no ads or sponsored recommendations and does not sell its own credit cards, loans or savings accounts.

TechCrunch noted that OpenAI launched similar personal finance tools in ChatGPT in May 2026, which let users connect financial accounts and ask about spending and planning. Anthropic said it is exploring ways for Claude to work with licensed professionals and regulated firms, and invited banks and wealth managers to get in touch.

The launch drew a public complaint from investor Anthony Pompliano, whose startup Silvia markets itself as a personal AI chief financial officer. In a post on X described by Decrypt, he accused Anthropic of seeking details about how Silvia was built and called the new feature a Claude wrapper posing as a finance product. Decrypt did not report a response from Anthropic to those claims.

The feature moves Claude from work tasks into one of the most personal kinds of data people have. The read-only design and the promise not to train on hub conversations address the obvious worries, but the value for users will depend on how accurate the categorization is and how much they trust a chatbot with two years of their transactions.

The beta is limited to paying US subscribers for now, so the next signal is whether Anthropic opens it to more plans or countries, and whether it follows through on partnerships with regulated financial firms.
